solution: Both terms have the same number in front of the cube, so take out the common factor ${=c}$ first: ${=c}x^{3} {=op} {=c}y^{3} = {=c}(x^{3} {=op} y^{3})$
The bracket is a {=kind} of two cubes, because $x^{3} = (x)^{3}$ and $y^{3} = (y)^{3}$. The cube roots are $x$ and $y$, and $x^{3} {=op} y^{3} = (x {=op} y)(x^{2} {=op2} xy + y^{2})$
Put the common factor back in front of the factorised bracket: ${=c}(x^{3} {=op} y^{3}) = {=c}(x {=op} y)(x^{2} {=op2} xy + y^{2})$

proposed_misconceptions.label: Drops the common factor
proposed_misconceptions.description: Takes the common factor out and factorises the bracket, but leaves the factor out of the final answer.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Wrong signs in the trinomial
proposed_misconceptions.description: Uses the sign pattern of the other identity: writes x^2 - xy + y^2 for a difference of cubes, or x^2 + xy + y^2 for a sum of cubes.

notes: x and y stay fixed so the marker variables are fixed. Coefficient c is never 1 and never 8 (a perfect cube would let a solver also write it inside the brackets, e.g. (2x+2y)(4x^2-4xy+4y^2), which is a different shape of the same polynomial). Instances: 8 coefficients times sum or difference = 16. The solution is the book's we16 method on the simplest cubes (ex1-9-6).
